analysis.one_liner: Shields states, local governments, and tribes from Clean Air Act liability for emissions caused by natural events, accidents, war, or terrorism.
analysis.headline: The bill got no cosponsors and no committee hearing or vote; it died in a House subcommittee when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have added a provision to the Clean Air Act saying that states, their political subdivisions, and tribes could not be held liable under the law for emissions and their byproducts that result from acts of nature (such as volcanic eruptions and dust storms), accidents, war, terrorism, or fires occurring outside their jurisdiction related to land clearing, agriculture, and ecological restoration and management [S2][S3]. It never advanced past its initial committee referrals [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: State, tribal, and local governments would gain a blanket Clean Air Act liability shield for emissions tied to natural events, accidents, war, terrorism, and certain fires beyond their borders. That protection would chiefly spare these governments from lawsuits or enforcement actions over emissions and byproducts such as wildfire smoke and dust crossing into their jurisdictions [S2][S3]. Because governments are rarely held liable for genuinely natural emissions anyway, the practical benefit would have been modest.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would add a new subsection to Section 307 of the Clean Air Act stating that states, their political subdivisions, and tribes 'shall not be held liable under this Act' for emissions and their byproducts resulting from acts of nature — including volcanic eruptions and dust storms — accident, war, terrorism, or fires occurring beyond their jurisdiction related to land clearing, agriculture, and ecological restoration and management [S3].
The provision's effect is limited to liability 'under this Act' — the Clean Air Act — so it would not immunize governments from other environmental or tort claims [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Anyone exposed to emissions from the covered events — such as smoke from cross-border wildfires or dust storms — who might otherwise seek accountability from a state, local government, or tribe under the Clean Air Act would lose that avenue. The cost is small in practice, because the Clean Air Act rarely imposes liability on governments for natural events to begin with [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The liability shield could reduce accountability under the Clean Air Act: emissions tied to fires 'beyond its jurisdiction related to land clearing, agriculture and ecological restoration and management' — for example, smoke crossing state lines from managed burns or wildfire — could go unaddressed, and affected residents and downwind governments would have no federal claim against the responsible government entity [S3].

The bill is very broad in its exemptions — covering accidents, war, and terrorism in addition to natural events — without defining how much of an emission event must be attributable to those causes before the shield applies, which could invite disputes over whether a government's own actions contributed to the emissions [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill had little practical effect: no cosponsors signed on, neither committee of referral ever acted on it, and the Clean Air Act does not ordinarily impose liability on states or tribes for genuinely natural emissions, so the problem it addressed was narrow [S4][S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stakes on both sides are low. The bill would have given state, local, and tribal governments a modest liability shield covering natural events, accidents, war, terrorism, and certain out-of-jurisdiction fires, while giving residents a modestly weaker tool to hold those governments accountable under the Clean Air Act [S2][S3]. Because the measure never reached a hearing or vote and had no cosponsors, its real-world effect was zero; the record mainly shows a single-sponsored bill that did not attract support within its own party or from across the aisle [S4][S5].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, sent to the Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee about a week later, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Paul introduced the bill on April 30, 2003, and it was referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the House Judiciary Committee [S5].
On May 9, 2003, the bill was referred to the Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee of the Energy and Commerce Committee; that was the last action in the record [S5].
The bill had no cosponsors at any point, and neither the full committees nor the subcommittee held a hearing or markup, so the bill died at the end of the 108th Congress on January 3, 2005 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody much changed position. Because the bill never advanced, state, local, and tribal governments did not gain the liability shield, and people exposed to emissions from natural events and cross-border fires kept the Clean Air Act framework as it stood.

for.name: Rep. Ron Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 30, 2003 to add a Clean Air Act liability shield for states, local governments, and tribes

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee on May 9, 2003 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral the day it was introduced and never acted on it

sides.party_line_note: There was no floor vote and no committee vote, and the bill had zero cosponsors, so no party bloc ever took a recorded position on it [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have given these governments a blanket Clean Air Act liability shield for emissions from natural events, accidents, war, terrorism, and certain fires beyond their borders [S3]. It reduces their exposure to enforcement and lawsuits, but also reduces the accountability residents have against them for covered emissions; the measure never became law.
